title: Bringing a Dead 1979 Datsun Back to Life | Part 3: Brakes
creator: Rusty Knuckle Garage
description:
Part 3 of the Datsun 280ZX revival. Seized calipers, rotted lines, and a master cylinder that's been dry since the nineties.

sentences.t: Welcome back to the garage, this is part three of the Datsun build, and today it's brakes.
If you missed the last one, we got her running, which was amazing, but she cannot currently stop, which is less amazing.
So the plan is front calipers, the rear drums, all the hard lines, and the master cylinder.
Let's start up front.
I've got the wheel off, and you can see the caliper here is just completely crusted over.
I'm going to crack the bleeder screw first, see if any fluid comes out.
Nothing.
Not a drop, which tells me the line is either clogged or completely empty.
Let's get the caliper off, two bolts, and these have been on here for forty years, so penetrating oil and patience.
There we go, and, oh yeah, look at that piston, it's seized solid.
Honestly, I'm not even going to try to rebuild these, new remanufactured calipers are about forty bucks each.
Alright, before we get into the hard lines, which is the part I'm dreading, a quick word from the sponsor of today's video, Ridge.
Ridge makes these slim metal wallets, and I've been carrying this one for about a year now.
It holds up to twelve cards and some cash with this little clip on the back, and it's way thinner than the leather brick I used to sit on.
It's also got RFID blocking, so nobody can scan your cards from your back pocket.
And the best part for me, it's aluminum, so when I'm lying under a car with it in my pocket, it's not getting crushed or soaked in oil.
They've got a lifetime warranty, and if you don't like it, you can return it within forty five days.
Go to ridge dot com slash knuckle and use code KNUCKLE for ten percent off.
That's ridge dot com slash knuckle, link in the description.
Okay, hard lines.
So the original lines on this car run along the frame rail, and they're steel, and they are rotten.
You can see right here, it's bubbled and flaking, and if I press on it with a screwdriver, yep, it went right through.
So all of these are coming out, and I'm going to bend new ones from copper nickel, which is much easier to work with and won't rust.
The trick is to take the old line out in as few pieces as possible, so you can use it as a template.
I'm laying it on the bench, and I'll just follow the bends with the new line, using the tubing bender for the tight ones.
And then flaring the ends, which takes a bit of practice.
This is a double flare, you fold the end over on itself so it seals properly against the fitting.
That one's good, nice and even.
One down, five to go.
I'll speed this part up, because it took me most of Saturday.
Alright, all the lines are in, and now the master cylinder.
The old one's basically a fossil, so new one's going on, and I'm bench bleeding it first so I don't get air in the whole system.
Then fill her up and bleed every corner, starting with the one furthest from the master, that's the rear passenger side.
Pump, hold, open, close.
And there's fluid, clean fluid, no bubbles.
Okay, moment of truth, let's roll her out and try them.
And she stops.
She actually stops, that is a huge relief.
Big thanks again to Ridge for sponsoring this one, if you want a wallet that'll survive a garage, use code KNUCKLE for ten percent off at ridge dot com slash knuckle.
Next week is suspension, and the bushings on this thing are basically dust, so that'll be fun.
See you then.
